title: Apple's iPhone Duo Is Here: Dos and Don'ts for Your First Folding Phone
excerpt: Apple's first folding phone reaches stores on Friday at $1,999. The Associated Press's One Tech Tip collects the care rules that apply to the Duo and every foldable: nothing between the screens, no backward bends, and keep it away from keys, coins and crumbs.
body:
• Apple's iPhone Duo, the company's first folding phone, arrives in stores on Friday, priced from $1,999.
  • A folding display is a mechanical system: every open and close flexes the inner panel along its crease and works a hinge of more than 100 components.
  • The AP's rules are simple: never bend the phone backward, never force it open or shut, and never close it on anything — a coin, card or key trapped between the screens can puncture the display.
  • Reviewers rate the Duo's hardware highly but flag its price, the lack of a telephoto camera and Touch ID instead of Face ID as the main trade-offs.

Apple's first folding phone arrives in stores on Friday, bringing a flexible display to iPhone buyers for the first time. The form factor also brings a new set of ways to break an expensive phone, which is why the Associated Press devoted its One Tech Tip column this week to the dos and don'ts of folding phones.

The Duo, displayed at Apple's September 9 announcement in Cupertino, is a passport-shaped device that opens into a 7.6-inch inner display, with a 5.4-inch outer screen for use while closed. It starts at $1,999 — the most Apple has ever charged for an iPhone — and reviewers have praised its near-invisible crease and hinge while noting the trade-offs: no telephoto camera, Touch ID rather than Face ID, and the weight of the heaviest iPhone to date, according to Gizmodo's review.

The Rules That Matter

The core of the AP advisory, by Kelvin Chan, is narrow and specific: do not bend a folding phone backward, and do not use excessive force when opening or closing it. As Shattered's summary puts it, a folding display is a mechanical system first and a screen second — every fold flexes the panel along its crease and works the hinge assembly underneath.

https://x.com/PCMag/status/2113306723582620013

"Ignore the "close it empty" rule once, with a coin in the fold, and the repair bill will make the $1,999 purchase price look like the smaller number."

The rest of the guidance comes from the makers who have sold foldables for years. Google recommends avoiding contact with "crumbs, fingernails and sharp objects." Samsung advises making sure there is nothing between the screens — a card, a coin or a key — that could "scratch or puncture the main screen," and notes that the strong magnets along a foldable's edges attract exactly that kind of metal debris. Honor, which sells foldables outside North America, recommends not opening or closing its phones in extreme cold, when the screen can become brittle, and not leaving a phone closed for a long time, which stresses the screen and hinge.

Why This Launch Is Different

No previous iPhone launch needed a care advisory, because no previous iPhone had a joint. Foldable veterans at Samsung, Google and Honor learned these rules across a decade of devices; Apple's buyers are meeting them on day one, on the most expensive phone the company sells. The full checklist is in the card above — follow it, and the Duo's hinge and crease should outlast the phone's software support. Ignore the "close it empty" rule once, with a coin in the fold, and the repair bill will make the $1,999 purchase price look like the smaller number.
